s1loc: Cwmbran sits at the heart of Torfaen's charity and volunteer scene. The Eastern Valley Foodbank, part of the Trussell network, runs distribution from Ebenezer Evangelical Church and other sites, replenished by volunteers and supported by the big food-redistribution networks. Connect Torfaen and the Torfaen Voluntary Alliance link residents to local foodbanks, while Citizens Advice Torfaen issues vouchers. St David's Hospice Care, one of the UK's largest hospice-at-home providers, runs its warehouse and donation centre at Ty Coch and shops across the area.

The sector here runs at every size. Big regional charities like St David's Hospice Care fund care through a network of more than thirty shops and central buying, while small community groups, foodbanks, pantries and volunteer-run projects keep going on a shoestring across Cwmbran, Pontnewydd, Croesyceiliog and St Dials. Citizens Advice and mutual-aid groups round out the picture. We are glad to kit out the national charity with a trade account and the one-room foodbank with direct online ordering, no minimum.

Beyond food aid, Cwmbran has a busy charity-shop strip on Commercial Street and around the Cwmbran Centre on The Parade, where St David's and other names raise funds. Connect Torfaen and the Torfaen Voluntary Alliance broker volunteering across neighbourhoods like Fairwater, Greenmeadow and Llanyrafon, matching residents to befriending, driving and sorting roles. Community pantries, church-run lunch clubs and small mutual-aid groups operate quietly in Two Locks and Coed Eva, often staffed entirely by neighbours giving their time.

s1loc: Christchurch has a tight-knit charity and volunteer scene. Christchurch Food Bank+, a Christchurch Fellowship of Churches initiative run with Faithworks Wessex, operates from St Joseph's church in Purewell, handing out food parcels staffed by volunteers from local churches. Alongside it, the Christchurch Community Partnership leads a hot-meals scheme cooked by volunteer chefs. The big food-redistribution and foodbank networks supply much of the stock, and Lewis-Manning Hospice Care runs a charity shop on the High Street to fund local care.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities such as Lewis-Manning Hospice Care and Julia's House children's hospice raise money through shops and central buying, while small community groups, foodbanks, pantries and volunteer-run projects work on a shoestring across Purewell, Highcliffe, Mudeford and Burton. Christchurch Community Partnership tackles social isolation with a handful of staff and many volunteers. We are happy to supply the national charity through a trade account and the one-room foodbank direct online, no minimum.

Christchurch's High Street and Bargates carry a strong charity-shop presence, with hospice and community names raising vital income from donated goods. Volunteers from the Christchurch Fellowship of Churches run befriending and community schemes, and volunteer drivers deliver meals to isolated residents in Somerford, Jumpers and Stanpit. Smaller mutual-aid and church-led lunch clubs operate quietly across the town, while the Help and Kindness directory connects Dorset residents to roles, keeping local volunteer-run projects staffed week to week.

s1loc: Romford anchors Havering's charity and volunteer network. The Collier Row and Romford Foodbank, part of the Trussell network, runs from The Ascension Church, Romford Baptist Church and St Edward's, kept going by around thirty regular volunteers. The Salvation Army runs a community pantry, and a council-backed Community Hub stocks an affordable food pantry largely supplied through FareShare. The Havering Volunteer Centre partners all three Trussell foodbanks across the borough, matching residents to roles.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional names such as Saint Francis Hospice fund care through fourteen-plus shops and central buying, while small community groups, foodbanks, pantries and volunteer-run projects keep going on a shoestring across Collier Row, Harold Hill, Rainham and Gidea Park. Peabody's community hub and church-led pantries fill the gaps. We are glad to kit out the national charity through a trade account and the one-room foodbank direct online, no minimum.

Saint Francis Hospice runs general and furniture shops on South Street and Hilldene Avenue, part of a chain stretching across Havering, Barking and Dagenham, and Brentwood. The Havering Volunteer Centre brokers volunteering from its borough base, placing people into sorting, driving and befriending roles. Salvation Army community hubs, church-run pantries and small mutual-aid groups operate across Romford Town, Marshalls Park and Rise Park, with most stock donated by supermarkets and stretched by volunteers who give their time freely.

s1loc: Barnet has a dense web of charity and volunteer activity. Christ Church Food Bank works from the Open Door Centre, Burnt Oak Community Food Bank opens fortnightly, and the Claremont Road Food Hub, set up by Jesus House, Claremont Free Church and UK Mutual Aid, cooks and delivers meals and parcels across the borough. North London Hospice serves Barnet, Enfield and Haringey, while Mutual Aid Barnet feeds around eighty-six people a week and the big food-redistribution networks keep shelves stocked.

The sector here runs at every size. Regional charities like North London Hospice and the children's hospice the Ark raise money through shops and central buying, while small community groups, foodbanks, pantries and volunteer-run projects work on a shoestring across Burnt Oak, Childs Hill, Finchley and New Barnet. Barnet Together and the Young Barnet Foundation channel grants through the Barnet Community Response Fund. We are happy to supply the national charity through a trade account and the one-room foodbank direct online, no minimum.

Childs Hill food bank, set up by local people with All Saints' Church, and a string of church-led hubs keep neighbourhoods fed. Volunteering Barnet matches residents to roles across the borough, and Engage Barnet supports community and voluntary organisations with advice and small grants. Charity shops along the High Barnet and East Finchley parades raise hospice income, while mutual-aid groups and food hubs run on volunteer labour in Hendon, Colindale and Whetstone, often delivering parcels door to door to isolated households.

s1loc: Paignton sits within Torbay's active charity and volunteer scene. The Paignton Community Larder, founded in 2017, runs as a foodbank and social supermarket serving families and individuals in crisis, with volunteers sorting and distributing food. It works alongside the Torbay Food Alliance, a partnership of community foodbanks covering Paignton, Torquay and Brixham. Rowcroft Hospice, the bay's local hospice, funds its care through charity shops and is supplied in part by the big food-redistribution networks.

The sector here runs at every size. Regional charities like Rowcroft Hospice raise money through shops across Paignton, Torquay, Brixham and Newton Abbot plus central buying, while small community groups, foodbanks, pantries and volunteer-run projects keep going on a shoestring across Preston, Goodrington, Clifton and Roselands. The Torbay Food Alliance ties the smaller projects together. We are glad to kit out the national charity through a trade account and the one-room larder direct online, no minimum.

Rowcroft Hospice runs shops on Dartmouth Road and in the town centre, two of which sell furniture and white goods, each staffed by a manager and a committed volunteer team. Volunteering at Rowcroft is open from age fourteen in shops, drawing in retirees and young people alike. The Paignton Community Larder relies on volunteers for food distribution, sorting and community engagement, and church-led pantries and mutual-aid groups operate quietly across Blatchcombe, Collaton St Mary and Hookhills.

s1loc: Kirkcaldy has a well-rooted charity and volunteer scene. Kirkcaldy Foodbank Charity runs three sites at New Volunteer House on East Fergus Place, Link Living at Westbridge Mill and the Linton Lane Centre, and is unusual in Fife for allowing self-referral. Frontline volunteers greet visitors and packers prepare parcels. Greener Kirkcaldy runs weekly community meals supplied with surplus food from FareShare and Yules, and Fife Voluntary Action coordinates cost-of-living support across the town.

The sector here runs at every size. National and regional charities raise money through High Street shops and central buying, while small community groups, foodbanks, pantries and volunteer-run projects keep going on a shoestring across Templehall, Gallatown, Sinclairtown and Dysart. The Kirkcaldy Community Hub at the Mercat Shopping Centre runs a community fridge, larder and pantry with no referral needed. We are happy to supply the national charity through a trade account and the one-room foodbank direct online, no minimum.

Greener Kirkcaldy anchors much of the town's volunteer-led food and community work, from community meals to learning projects, drawing on FareShare-redistributed stock and a roster of local volunteers. Fife Voluntary Action brokers volunteering and supports cost-of-living projects, while church-led pantries and mutual-aid groups operate across Pathhead, Smeaton and the Linton Lane area. Charity shops along the High Street raise funds for national and Scottish charities, staffed largely by volunteers who sort, price and sell donated goods week in, week out.

s1loc: Batley has a hard-working charity and volunteer scene. Batley Food Bank, a registered charity, opens five days a week providing parcels for people in Batley and North Kirklees, with volunteers from all walks of life. Mount Pleasant Islamic Trust has supported Batley Food Bank and Fusion in Dewsbury for years through its Kind Connections project. FareShare Yorkshire, working from Leeds, supplies many of the area's food providers and runs a FareShare Go service drawing surplus from Tesco and Asda.

The sector here runs at every size. Regional charities like The Kirkwood, the hospice for Kirklees, raise money through shops and central buying, while small community groups, foodbanks, pantries and volunteer-run projects keep going on a shoestring across Batley Carr, Staincliffe, Birstall and Heckmondwike. The West Yorkshire Food Poverty Network and Kirklees Council tie the smaller projects together. We are glad to kit out the national charity through a trade account and the one-room foodbank direct online, no minimum.

The Kirkwood runs a charity shop on Commercial Street in Batley and a cluster of shops, a furniture store and an eBay hub at Sandsmill in nearby Mirfield, each leaning on volunteers. The Batley Salvation Army hub pairs a charity shop with a friendly cafe, doubling as a community space. Mount Pleasant Islamic Trust, church-led pantries and mutual-aid groups operate across Mount Pleasant, Wilton and Soothill, with FareShare-redistributed stock keeping volunteer-run projects fed throughout North Kirklees.
